fun_facts: A bonito under thirty inches can burst to around 40 mph, a tuna-like body built for short, hard sprints rather than the long, steady cruising of its bigger scombrid cousins.

It grows fast and dies young: most of a bonito's length is packed on in its first two or three years, and few live past five, a strikingly short lifespan for a fish that reaches this size that quickly.

Anglers up and down the Atlantic coast regularly hook a bonito while trolling for something else entirely, then re-rig it whole as live or dead bait for the much larger tuna, marlin, or shark they were actually after.

measures.label: Total length
measures.help: Tip of the snout to the tip of the tail, with the tail lobes pinched together for a straight-line measurement.

vocabs.label: Sex
vocabs.help: Atlantic bonito cannot be sexed externally in the field; unknown is the normal answer.

not_taggable.reason: a fish in poor condition or bleeding is unlikely to survive release, so tagging it wastes the tag and the reward

must_release.reason: Atlantic bonito carry no dedicated South Carolina or federal recreational size limit; SCDNR's general 12-inch minimum for tagging-eligible marine game fish applies instead
